extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science; scientists and philosophers interested in scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual guidance for forming, interpreting, and judging scientific laws and the scientific method — distinguishing scientific (descriptive) laws from other senses of 'law', the conditions for their universality, and how they are tested and progressed. Uses historical examples (planetary theories) and philosophical discussion (Stoics, Hooker, Newton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of scientific law (mental shorthand)
rubrics_metrics.description: A law in science is a 'resume in mental shorthand' which replaces a lengthy description of sequences among our sense-impressions; it is essentially a product of the human mind and has no meaning apart from man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific laws are mental formulas that briefly describe sequences of observed phenomena (example: Newton's law of gravitation as a method of describing planetary motion). Emphasise that the law is a created description rather than an external command or metaphysical given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the two senses of 'natural law'
rubrics_metrics.description: Two senses must be separated: (1) the old/nomic sense — the mere concatenation or routine of perceptions (a sequence of sense-impressions); (2) the scientific sense — the mental formula which gives brief expression to those sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using 'natural law' be explicit which sense is intended; confusion of the two (as in Stoic and Hooker writings) leads to category mistakes mixing descriptive and prescriptive notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil/moral law versus scientific law distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil (or moral) law involves command and duty, varies with age and society, and is valid for special communities; scientific law is descriptive, involves no command or duty, and is valid for all normal human beings (relative to our faculties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat civil law as a social/natural product historically traceable to customs; do not conflate prescriptive legal norms with descriptive natural laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid projecting human conceptions as external reasons (argument from design fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer that reason exists behind phenomena merely because human reason can formulate laws; projecting mental constructs into an unconditioned outside world (as the Stoics/Hooker did) is unwarranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the origin of such fallacies: show how classification and conceptualising by the human mind can lead to projecting reason into nature. Science must explain why the fallacy arises rather than merely dismissing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newton's canon — forbid seeking superfluous causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not seek new or superfluous causes for natural phenomena until it is shown that known causes cannot account for them; avoid positing unknown reasons without demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Newton's regula philosophandi as a guiding methodological canon: only introduce new causes when necessity is demonstrated. This is framed as an economy of thought and central to the scientific method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for a 'fundamental' law: breadth and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider the range of phenomena embraced and the simpler the statement of the law, the more nearly it approaches a 'fundamental law of nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidate laws by how many phenomena they classify and by the simplicity/conciseness of their formulation. Historical example: progression from Ptolemy → Copernicus → Kepler → Newton shows increasing breadth and simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific progress as replacement by wider generalisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier formulae are not necessarily wrong but are 'first approximations' that get replaced by briefer, more accurate, and more wide-embracing statements as knowledge widens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat older theories as approximations valid within limited regimes (neglecting small quantities); prefer theories that extend to wider ranges without undue complication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical test is the final arbiter (laws ↔ hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only final test of the truth or sufficiency of any law is the actual comparison of the formula's results with the facts themselves — historical observation or physical experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scientific law must always be testable and is liable to revert to hypothesis as perceptive powers increase; robustness under universal experience is the hallmark of truth (Herschel quote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of scientific law is relative to human faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality and 'absolute' character of scientific law are conditioned by (1) the perceptive faculty and (2) the reflective faculty; they hold only for 'normal' human beings whose faculties are substantially similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of universality by checking the assumptions about the sameness of perceptive and reasoning faculties across observers; recognise that minds outside the normal range (e.g., delusional) may not share the same laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and concept-formation as basis of law-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists form conceptions from sense-impressions by combining, isolating, and generalising; from classification they pass to formulae that describe sequences and relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise disciplined imagination and careful classification (example: Kepler's laws stemming from Tycho Brahe's observations) as essential steps in producing laws. Expect some conceptions (atoms, molecules) to be 'supersensuous' — intellectual constructs used for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish physicist's 'supersensuous' concepts from metaphysical ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicists' supersensuous concepts (e.g., atoms/molecules) are intellectual conceptions not yet direct sense-impressions and may later become 'real'; metaphysicians' supersensuous asserts unconditioned existence apart from human faculties — an unprovable dogma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating useful theoretical constructs (which are methodological tools) with metaphysical claims of independent reality without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of thought and methodological humility
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific laws economise thought by summarising routines of perception; scientists should be humble that laws may be superseded and must be continually tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer parsimonious explanations; remain open to revision as perceptive powers and data increase. Critically study fallacies and historical examples to sharpen methodological insight.
